questions.context:
A galvanometer is an instrument used to show the direction and strength of the current passing through it. In a galvanometer, a coil placed in a magnetic field experiences a torque and hence gets deflected when a current passes through it. The name is derived from the surname of Italian scientist L. Galvani, who in 1791 discovered that electric current makes a dead frog's leg jerk. A spring attached with the coil provides a counter torque.
In equilibrium, the deflecting torque is balanced by the restoring torque of the spring and we have :
\(\mathrm{NBAI} = k\phi\)
where N is the total number of turns in the coil
A is the area of cross-section of each turn
B is the radial magnetic field
k is the torsional constant of the spring
\(\phi\) is the angular deflection of the coil
As the current \((I_g)\) which produces full scale deflection in the galvanometer is very small, the galvanometer cannot as such be used to measure current in electric circuits. A small resistance, called shunt, of a suitable value is connected with the galvanometer to convert it into an ammeter of desired range. By using a higher resistance, a galvanometer can also be converted into a voltmeter.

questions.subtopic: Photoelectric Effect and its Experimental Study
questions.context:
Einstein explained photoelectric effect on the basis of Planck's quantum theory, where light travels in the form of small bundles of energy called photons. The energy of each photon is \(h
u\), where \(
u\) is the frequency of incident light and h is Planck's constant. The number of photons in a beam of light determines the intensity of the incident light. A photon incident on a metal surface transfers its total energy \(h
u\) to a free electron in the metal. A part of this energy is used in ejecting the electron from the metal and is called its work function. The rest of the energy is carried by the ejected electron as its kinetic energy.
questions.stem: Which of the following graphs shows the variation of photoelectric current I with the intensity of light ?

options.label: A
options.text: A plot of I (vertical axis) against Intensity (horizontal axis, arrowed) : a straight line starting on the I-axis and falling steadily to meet the Intensity-axis.

options.label: B
options.text: A plot of I (vertical axis) against Intensity (horizontal axis, arrowed) : a horizontal straight line, parallel to the Intensity-axis and above it.

options.label: C
options.text: A plot of I (vertical axis) against Intensity (horizontal axis, arrowed) : a straight line from the origin O rising with a constant positive slope.

options.label: D
options.text: A plot of I (vertical axis) against Intensity (horizontal axis, arrowed) : a curve rising steeply from the origin O and then flattening to a horizontal asymptote.

questions._figure: REQUIRED — all four options are DRAWN GRAPHS and the stem names none of them. Each option's axes, labels and curve shape are described in its option text; that is a lossless reading rather than an approximation, and it does not state the answer, because the discrimination the question tests is the physics (how photocurrent depends on intensity), not the reading of the picture. Page idx 20.

questions.context:
Einstein explained photoelectric effect on the basis of Planck's quantum theory, where light travels in the form of small bundles of energy called photons. The energy of each photon is \(h
u\), where \(
u\) is the frequency of incident light and h is Planck's constant. The number of photons in a beam of light determines the intensity of the incident light. A photon incident on a metal surface transfers its total energy \(h
u\) to a free electron in the metal. A part of this energy is used in ejecting the electron from the metal and is called its work function. The rest of the energy is carried by the ejected electron as its kinetic energy.

questions.stem: Which of the following metals exhibits photoelectric effect with visible light ?

(i) Three batteries \(E_1\), \(E_2\) and \(E_3\) of emfs and internal resistances \((4\) V, \(2\ \Omega)\), \((2\) V, \(4\ \Omega)\) and \((6\) V, \(2\ \Omega)\) respectively are connected as shown in the figure. Find the values of the currents passing through batteries \(E_1\), \(E_2\) and \(E_3\).
(ii) The ends of six wires, each of resistance R \((= 10\ \Omega)\) are joined as shown in the figure. The points A and B of the arrangement are connected in a circuit. Find the value of the effective resistance offered by it to the circuit.
questions._figure: REQUIRED — TWO figures back this one row and both stems defer entirely to them ('as shown in the figure'). Sub-part (i): a rectangular circuit whose left and right sides are joined by three horizontal branches, one above the other, each carrying a battery cell symbol labelled \(E_1\), \(E_2\) and \(E_3\) from top to bottom. Sub-part (ii): six resistors each labelled R drawn as a triangle with a centre node — the three outer sides carry one R each (the bottom side runs between the marked terminals A and B) and three more R's run from the centre node to each vertex. The CELL POLARITIES in (i) and the exact vertex-to-node pairing in (ii) are DELIBERATELY WITHHELD, since the current directions and the bridge balance are what the question tests. Page idx 22.

questions.stem:
(i) Current I \((= 1\) A\()\) is passing through a copper rod \((n = 8{\cdot}5 \times 10^{28}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}})\) of varying cross-sections as shown in the figure. The areas of cross-section at points A and B along its length are \(1{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m^2}\) and \(2{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m^2}\) respectively. Calculate :
(I) the ratio of electric fields at points A and B.
(II) the drift velocity of free electrons at point B.
(ii) Two point charges \(q_1\) \((= 16\ \mu\mathrm{C})\) and \(q_2\) \((= 1\ \mu\mathrm{C})\) are placed at points \(\vec{r_1} = (3\) m\()\hat{i}\) and \(\vec{r_2} = (4\) m\()\hat{j}\). Find the net electric field \(\vec{E}\) at point \(\vec{r} = (3\) m\()\hat{i} + (4\) m\()\hat{j}\).
questions._figure: ILLUSTRATIVE — a tapering copper rod drawn in perspective, narrow at the left where the current I enters (arrow) and wider at the right where it leaves (arrow), with two hatched cross-sections marked A (nearer the narrow end) and B (nearer the wide end). Attached because it shows the geometry, but the row is answerable from the stem alone: BOTH cross-sectional areas are stated in words, so the drawing carries no quantity the text omits. Page idx 24.
questions._flag: Sub-parts (i) and (ii) belong to DIFFERENT chapters — (i) is Current Electricity (drift velocity, current density) and (ii) is Electric Charges and Fields (superposition of point-charge fields). Filed on Current Electricity, which carries 3 of the 5 marks and matches the branch it is an alternative to. Not a defect; recorded so the taxonomy choice is visible.

questions.stem:
(i) Define self-inductance of a coil. Derive the expression for the energy required to build up a current I in a coil of self-inductance L.
(ii) The currents passing through two inductors of self-inductances 10 mH and 20 mH increase with time at the same rate.
Draw graphs showing the variation of :
(I) the magnitude of emf induced with the rate of change of current in each inductor.
(II) the energy stored in each inductor with the current flowing through it.

(i) Define the term mutual inductance. Deduce the expression for the mutual inductance of two long coaxial solenoids of the same length having different radii and different number of turns.
(ii) The current through an inductor is uniformly increased from zero to 2 A in 40 s. An emf of 5 mV is induced during this period. Find the flux linked with the inductor at \(t = 10\) s.

(i) Draw a ray diagram of a reflecting telescope (Cassegrain) and explain the formation of image. State two important advantages that a reflecting telescope has over a refracting telescope.
(ii) In a refracting telescope, the focal length of the objective is 50 times the focal length of the eyepiece. When the final image is formed at infinity, the length of the tube is 102 cm. Find the focal lengths of the two lenses.

(i) Write any two advantages of a compound microscope over a simple microscope. Draw a ray diagram for the image formation at the near point by a compound microscope and explain it.
(ii) A thin planoconcave lens with its curved face of radius of curvature R is made of glass of refractive index \(n_1\). It is placed coaxially in contact with a thin equiconvex lens of same radius of curvature of refractive index \(n_2\). Obtain the power of the combination lens.
questions._flag: Sub-part (ii) is lens-maker's formula / power of a lens combination ('Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses') while sub-part (i) is the compound microscope. Filed on 'Optical Instruments' to match the branch it is an alternative to. Not a defect.
